newsitem.title: USA: Towers' Hoffenberg gets 20 year sentence.
newsitem.headline: Towers' Hoffenberg gets 20 year sentence.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, Law Correspondent

A federal judge sentenced Steven Hoffenberg, accused of masterminding the biggest financial swindle in U.S. history, to 20 years in prison Friday, saying the financier wreaked havoc on thousands of innocent lives.

U.S. District Judge Robert Sweet also ordered Hoffenberg, 52, the former head of scandal-ridden Towers Financial Corp., to pay $462,556,436 in restitution and a fine of $1 million. The judge had announced his plans to issue the stiff prison term earlier this week pending Friday's hearing.

The sentence applies to both a New York case, in which Hoffenberg defrauded more than 3,000 people, and a federal case transferred from Chicago in which he was charged with defrauding two insurance companies of more than $3 million.
Hoffenberg said he would appeal the sentence.

The flamboyant financier had run Towers, the bill-collection business that filed for bankruptcy protection from creditors in 1993, until it was discovered that he was using the company to operate what prosecutors called the largest Ponzi scheme ever in the United States.

Sweet said he had received hundreds of letters from victims describing how Hoffenberg's schemes had "wreaked havoc on innocent lives." He said the letters were from the "whole spectrum of America," including teachers, waitresses, bailiffs, firefighters, lawyers and auto mechanics.
He said some of the most heart-breaking letters were from elderly investors in their 70s and 80s who had lost their retirement savings and were forced to look for work.
"There has been tremendous suffering here," Sweet said.
"You have not accepted responsibility for these securities frauds," Sweet told Hoffenberg. "The responsibility for the situation is yours."
The judge said that while Hoffenberg is now indigent, it may be possible for him to come up with some of the money.

"He has demonstrated a capacity to pop up with plans and I suspect he has some even as we speak," said Sweet. He explained that Hoffenberg might sell his life story or come up with "some other business scheme, even from prison."

Hoffenberg gained wide-spread attention when he offered to rescue the financially ailing New York Post in January 1993. The deal unravelled when the Securities and Exchange Commission sued to freeze his assets. Even with that action, he continued to secretly run collection businesses and made an unsuccessful attempt to start a women's magazine.
In 1994 he agreed to a $60 million settlement with the SEC. The SEC later filed a contempt proceeding for non-payment. In 1995 he pleaded guilty to the criminal conspiracy and fraud charges.
Hoffenberg was arrested in February 1996 in Little Rock, Ark., after failing to meet new bail terms. He said at the time he was planning to run for the U.S. Senate.
He has remained in prison since last year. Prosecutors said that he was married shortly over a month ago.

During Friday's hearing, Hoffenberg unsuccessfully tried to convince Sweet that others involved in the Towers bankruptcy proceeding were responsible for the loss of funds and that he had been a great help to prosecutors investigating other securities frauds.
"I have accepted responsibility. I did plead guilty. I worked hard with everyone who asked me questions about recovering money," Hoffenberg said.

But Amy Millard, assistant U.S. attorney, said the stiff sentence was "richly deserved" and that Hoffenberg had stolen more than money. She said he had robbed investors of their "dreams, hopes, and financial security."
She said Hoffenberg had taken a small collection agency and through "massive looting" had turned it into a "bloated institution riddled with fraud."
Millard denied that Hoffenberg had assisted the government in its investigations.
"His statement is truly astonishing in its arrogance ... He has shown himself untrustworthy of belief over and over again," she said.

Hoffenberg recently asked to withdraw his guilty plea, claiming he was mentally unfit when he admitted to the fraud. Sweet denied his request. The judge said that while Hoffenberg has a history of mental illness, he also had the resources to cope with the problem but failed to do so.

Sweet said the central offence to which Hoffenberg pleaded guilty was a Ponzi scheme -- a fraudulent pyramid-type scheme that involves luring investors seeking high interest-rate returns and using the funds to pay off earlier investors.
Hoffenberg was accused of selling $450 million in fraudulent notes and bonds and using some funds from later investors to pay interest owed to earlier ones.

The rest of the money was used to run the Post for several months and to operate a financial empire with inflated revenues and profits under the appearance of being a major health care financing company.
